quiz.question: Which statement best describes a system call in an operating system?
options: An ordinary function call that executes entirely within the application's user address space
A controlled request for a privileged kernel service that crosses the user/kernel boundary
An asynchronous hardware signal triggered by an external NVMe storage device
A mandatory context switch to another process in all execution paths
quiz.explanation: A system call is an intentional, controlled interface mechanism by which user-space programs request services from the privileged operating system kernel across the hardware privilege boundary.

quiz.question: What fundamentally distinguishes a hardware interrupt from a synchronous CPU exception?
options: A hardware interrupt arrives asynchronously relative to the executing instruction stream
An interrupt always originates directly from user-space application code
CPU exceptions never transition into privileged kernel code
They are completely identical in origin, timing, and vector routing on all CPU architectures
quiz.explanation: Hardware interrupts are generated asynchronously by external hardware components (timers, network cards, disks) regardless of what instruction the CPU is currently executing. Exceptions are synchronous and caused by the execution of the current instruction (page faults, division by zero).

quiz.question: Why must the kernel strictly validate all user-supplied pointers during a system call?
options: Because user memory automatically becomes read-only upon entering the kernel
Because user pointers may be invalid, unmapped, point to kernel memory, or be concurrently modified to cause security exploits
Because pointers are automatically converted to physical addresses by hardware at syscall entry
Validation is only required for filesystem operations, never for memory buffers
quiz.explanation: User pointers cannot be trusted. If the kernel blindly dereferenced user pointers without verification (or without copy_from_user), malicious user code could read or overwrite arbitrary kernel memory, bypassing all OS isolation.

quiz.question: What is the primary architectural danger of a bug in a Loadable Kernel Module (LKM) in Linux?
options: It can only terminate the user process that loaded it
Because LKMs execute in privileged Ring 0, a bug can corrupt shared kernel memory or compromise the entire host system
LKMs execute in a restricted sandbox and cannot access host RAM
It affects only the specific source file of the module
quiz.explanation: Linux is a monolithic kernel. Loadable kernel modules execute with full Ring 0 privileges in kernel space. A null-pointer dereference, buffer overflow, or wild write in a kernel module can corrupt any kernel data structure or trigger an immediate kernel panic.

quiz.question: Why do microkernel architectures (such as seL4 or MINIX 3) offer superior fault isolation compared to monolithic kernels?
options: All device drivers and filesystems execute in a single shared privileged address space
Most traditional kernel services (drivers, filesystems, networking) run as isolated user-space processes
Microkernels eliminate all CPU context switches and IPC overhead
Microkernels automatically prevent all software security vulnerabilities
quiz.explanation: In a microkernel, only core mechanisms (scheduling, basic memory primitives, IPC) remain in Ring 0. Drivers and filesystems run as ordinary unprivileged user-space processes. If a device driver crashes, it does not bring down the kernel and can simply be restarted.

quiz.question: Why is the xv6 operating system widely studied in operating systems engineering alongside production Linux?
options: xv6 is a binary drop-in replacement for enterprise Linux distributions
Its compact, readable codebase allows learners to trace real end-to-end kernel mechanisms that are obscured by Linux's vast complexity
The system call implementation and device driver models in xv6 are 100% identical to Linux
xv6 operates entirely in user space without requiring hardware or emulator support
quiz.explanation: While Linux contains tens of millions of lines of code with complex architecture-specific optimizations, MIT's xv6 implements core Unix principles (processes, paging, system calls, spinlocks, filesystems) in under 10,000 lines of clean C, making kernel mechanisms directly readable and traceable.

theorySections.title: 1. Kernel Responsibilities and Subsystem Boundaries
paragraphs: The privileged core · Subsystem contracts · Monolithic address spaces · Hardware coordination

The kernel is the privileged core of an operating system. While user-space applications are strictly isolated inside virtual address spaces, the kernel executes with unrestricted hardware access, managing CPU registers, page table roots, physical memory, and device controllers.
Maintains PCB / task_struct records, per-core runqueues, context switching, CPU affinity, and preemption.
Constructs hierarchical page tables, handles demand page faults, manages buddy physical allocators and slab/slub caches.
Translates file paths via inodes and dentries, manages dirty page writeback, and queues I/O through blk-mq.

In a monolithic operating system like Linux, subsystem boundaries (e.g. between the VFS and the NVMe driver) are enforced only by C code conventions, not by hardware isolation. A null-pointer dereference or stray pointer in a device driver can corrupt scheduling queues or filesystem state across the entire computer.

theorySections.title: 3. Interrupts, Exceptions, and Privilege Transitions
paragraphs: Traps vs Syscalls vs IRQs · x86 Ring 0/Ring 3 · ARM EL0/EL1 · Top-half vs Bottom-half (softirqs)
Execution transitions into privileged kernel space via three distinct architectural events:
Synchronous, intentional software requests (syscall, ecall). Application deliberately requests an OS service.
Synchronous, instruction-generated faults (e.g. Page Fault #14, Division by Zero #0). Can be recoverable or fatal (SIGSEGV).
Asynchronous electrical signals from peripherals (network packet arrival, NVMe completion, timer tick). Unrelated to current instruction.

theorySections.title: 5. Kernel Stacks, Synchronization, and Scheduling
paragraphs: Kernel stack boundaries · Spinlocks vs Mutexes · Interrupt-safety (spin_lock_irqsave) · Context switching

Every running process in Linux has two stacks: a large user-space stack (typically 8MB limit) and a small, fixed-size per-thread kernel stack (typically 8KB or 16KB). Because kernel stack space is precious, kernel code must never allocate large local arrays or use deep recursion.
Busy-waits in a tight CPU loop until the lock is freed. Never sleeps! Can be held in interrupt context. Critical sections must be as short as possible.
Sleeping lock. If the lock is held, the calling thread is placed on a wait queue and yields the CPU via schedule(). Strictly illegal in interrupt context!
Understand why raw spin_lock can trigger an unrecoverable kernel deadlock when interrupted by a hardware timer, and how spin_lock_irqsave prevents it.

theorySections.title: 6. Kernel Architecture Models: Monolithic, Microkernel & Hybrid
paragraphs: Linux vs seL4 / Mach · Fault isolation blast radius · Loadable Kernel Modules (LKMs) · Security risks
How should the boundary between privileged and unprivileged code be drawn?

All core services (Scheduler, MM, Filesystems, Network Stacks, Device Drivers) share one Ring 0 address space. Direct C function calls make it blisteringly fast, but a single driver crash can panic the whole OS.

Ring 0 contains only IPC, basic scheduling, and hardware traps (typically <10K lines of code). Filesystems, network stacks, and device drivers run as isolated user processes. A crashed driver is simply restarted.
Switch between Monolithic and Microkernel models. Click "Inject Driver Crash" to observe the difference between an OS-wide Kernel Panic and isolated user process recovery.
